method: The cut angle follows from the line of centres. With cue ball C, object ball O and the selected pocket P, the unit vector u points from O to P, and the ghost-ball centre is G = O - 2r u, where r is the ball radius. The cue ball must travel from C to G, so the cut angle is the angle between C to G and u: it is 0 for a straight shot and approaches 90 degrees as the hit gets thinner. An angle above 90 degrees means C lies on the pocket side of O, so a centre-ball hit cannot send the object ball toward that pocket. The contact point on the object ball is O - r u, the cue-ball travel is the distance from C to G, the object-ball travel is the distance from O to P, and the aim-line offset from the object ball's centre is 2r sin(cut). Standard American pool balls are 2.25 in (57.15 mm) in diameter; the playing surfaces are 78 x 39 in (7 ft), 88 x 44 in (8 ft) and 100 x 50 in (9 ft). Coordinates run from the bottom-left corner with x along the long rail, in inches or centimetres, and every ball centre must sit at least one radius inside the cushions. The model assumes a centre-ball hit with no side spin, no throw, no cushion contact and no pocket-jaw effects, so it is a planning aid rather than a prediction that a shot drops.
